theorem.proof_tex:
Fix \(N\geq N_0\), \(p\in\mathcal P\), and \(|\gamma|\leq G\).  Put
\[
 \delta=N^{-1/2},\qquad g=\gamma_N,
 \qquad b_g(x)=-dx-\nu\min\{x,g\},
 \qquad \overline G=G+1.
 \tag{1}
\]
By the definition of \(M_N\),
\[
 0\leq g-\gamma<\delta\leq1,
 \qquad |g|\leq\overline G.
 \tag{2}
\]
The compact rate assumptions give the strictly positive, uniform bounds
\[
 2c\leq d\leq2C,\qquad 3c\leq D\leq3C,\qquad
 q_*:=\frac{2c^2}{3C}\leq q=\frac{\lambda(\tau+\nu)}D\leq C.
 \tag{3}
\]
Also,
\[
 a(p)\geq\frac{c}{3C}\geq\beta,
 \qquad 1-a(p)\geq\frac{2c}{C+2c}\geq\beta.
\]
Writing \(r_0=(G+\sqrt{G^2+4\beta})/(2\beta)\), the definition of \(N_0\) gives \(\sqrt N\geq r_0\), and \(r_0\) is the positive root of \(\beta r^2-Gr-1=0\).  The quadratic is increasing on \([r_0,\infty)\), so
\[
 \beta N-G\sqrt N\geq1,
 \qquad
 1\leq M_N=\lceil Na(p)+\gamma\sqrt N\rceil\leq N-1.
\]
Thus the displayed birth and death rates are nonnegative, and their only unavailable boundary jumps have rate zero.  Every division by \(d,D,q\) below is valid.  The relevant state support is the finite lattice \(E_{1,N}=\{(k-Na)/\sqrt N:0\leq k\leq N\}\).  No rank, overlap, or limiting argument is used in this finite-\(N\) estimate.

We first obtain bounds for the diffusion Poisson solution uniformly for \(|g|\leq\overline G\).  The density in the piecewise Poisson construction satisfies
\[
 q\pi_g'(x)=b_g(x)\pi_g(x)
 \tag{4}
\]
on both sides of \(g\), and the density and its first derivative agree at \(g\), because \(b_g\) is continuous there.  Its displayed Gaussian branches have finite moments of every fixed order.  Hence integration by parts, with the Gaussian boundary terms equal to zero, gives
\[
 0=\int \mathcal L_g(x^2)\pi_g(x)\,dx
   =-2d\mathbb E_{\pi_g}X^2
     -2\nu\mathbb E_{\pi_g}\{X\min(X,g)\}+2q.
 \tag{5}
\]
For every real \(x,g\),
\[
 x\min(x,g)\geq-|g|\,|x|.
 \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, the left side is nonnegative when \(x\leq0\) or \(g\geq0\), except possibly when \(x>0>g\), in which case it equals \(xg=-|g||x|\).  If \(y_g=(\mathbb E_{\pi_g}X^2)^{1/2}\), equations (2), (3), (5), and (6), followed by Cauchy--Schwarz, imply
\[
 2c y_g^2\leq C+C\overline G y_g.
 \tag{7}
\]
Consequently
\[
 |m_g|\leq y_g\leq
 M_\pi:=\frac{C\overline G+\sqrt{C^2\overline G^2+8cC}}{4c}.
 \tag{8}
\]

For completeness, the global first-derivative bound used below follows directly from the primitive drift.  Couple two solutions of
\[
 dY_t=b_g(Y_t)\,dt+\sqrt{2q}\,dB_t
 \tag{9}
\]
with the same Brownian motion and initial states \(y>x\).  Since \(u\mapsto\min(u,g)\) is nondecreasing and one-Lipschitz,
\[
 -D(Y_t^y-Y_t^x)
 \leq b_g(Y_t^y)-b_g(Y_t^x)
 \leq-d(Y_t^y-Y_t^x).
 \tag{10}
\]
Until a first meeting time, the Brownian terms in (9) cancel, so the positive difference is absolutely continuous and satisfies (10) almost everywhere.  Gronwall's inequality gives the following bounds up to that time; the strictly positive lower bound rules out a finite meeting, so they hold for every \(t\geq0\):
\[
 e^{-Dt}(y-x)\leq Y_t^y-Y_t^x\leq e^{-dt}(y-x).
 \tag{11}
\]
Coupling one initial state to an independent stationary draw from \(\pi_g\) shows that
\[
 r_g(x):=\int_0^\infty\{\mathbb E_xY_t-m_g\}\,dt
 \tag{12}
\]
is absolutely convergent.  The semigroup identity
\[
 P_s r_g-r_g=-\int_0^sP_t(x-m_g)\,dt
 \tag{13}
\]
and dominated convergence yield \(-\mathcal L_g r_g=x-m_g\).  Fubini's theorem and stationarity give \(\int r_g\,d\pi_g=0\); absolute integrability follows from (11) and the finite first moment established above.  The centered solution is unique: the derivative of the difference of two solutions is a constant times \(1/\pi_g\) by (4), and the Gaussian tails make such a difference nonintegrable unless that constant is zero; centering then removes the remaining additive constant.  Thus (12) is the function \(h_g\) in the diffusion Poisson construction.  Integrating (11) over \(t\) and taking difference quotients therefore gives
\[
 \frac1D\leq h_g'(x)\leq\frac1d\leq\frac1{2c},
 \qquad x\in\mathbb R.
 \tag{14}
\]
This also independently verifies, on the one-step-enlarged window required by the ceiling in (2), the derivative control appearing in Theorem \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\).

Let
\[
 F_g(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x(u-m_g)\pi_g(u)\,du.
 \tag{15}
\]
The construction \(h_g'=-F_g/(q\pi_g)\), equation (4), and positivity of \(q\pi_g\) show that \(h_g'\) is continuously differentiable.  The Poisson equation can therefore be written pointwise as
\[
 qh_g''(x)=-(x-m_g)-b_g(x)h_g'(x).
 \tag{16}
\]
Because
\[
 |b_g(x)|\leq3C|x|+C\overline G,
 \tag{17}
\]
equations (3), (8), (14), and (16) give
\[
 |h_g''(x)|\leq C_1(1+|x|),
 \quad
 C_1:=q_*^{-1}\left\{1+M_\pi+\frac{3C+C\overline G}{2c}\right\}.
 \tag{18}
\]
On each open side of \(g\), differentiating (16) gives
\[
 qh_g'''(x)=-1-b_g'(x)h_g'(x)-b_g(x)h_g''(x),
 \qquad b_g'(x)\in\{-D,-d\}.
 \tag{19}
\]
It follows from (3), (14), (17), and (18) that, for almost every \(x\),
\[
 |h_g'''(x)|\leq C_2(1+x^2),
 \quad
 C_2:=q_*^{-1}\left\{1+\frac{3C}{2c}
       +2C_1(3C+C\overline G)\right\}.
 \tag{20}
\]
Both \(b_g\) and \(h_g'\) are continuous at \(g\), so (16) makes \(h_g''\) continuous there.  Since (19)--(20) hold on the two sides, \(h_g''\) is locally absolutely continuous across \(g\).  Taylor's formula with integral remainder is therefore valid on an interval that meets or crosses the kink, with the essential supremum in (20).  This is the step that prevents a kink-edge remainder of order one.

At \(x=(k-Na)/\sqrt N\), define the available birth and death rates
\[
 B_N(x)=\lambda(N-k),
 \qquad D_N^-(x)=\tau k+\nu\min\{k,M_N\}.
 \tag{21}
\]
Since \(k=Na+\sqrt N x\), \(M_N=Na+\sqrt N g\), and \(\lambda(1-a)=(\tau+\nu)a=q\), direct algebra gives the exact identities
\[
 \delta\{B_N(x)-D_N^-(x)\}=b_g(x),
 \tag{22}
\]
\[
 \frac{\delta^2}{2}\{B_N(x)+D_N^-(x)\}
 =q+\frac\delta2 r_g^N(x),
 \qquad
 r_g^N(x)=(\tau-\lambda)x+\nu\min(x,g).
 \tag{23}
\]
These identities also hold at \(k=0,N\), because the unavailable rate in (21) is then exactly zero.  Moreover,
\[
 B_N(x)+D_N^-(x)\leq3CN,
 \qquad
 |r_g^N(x)|\leq C_r(1+|x|),
 \quad C_r:=C(2+\overline G).
 \tag{24}
\]

Apply Taylor's formula only to available edges.  Equations (18) and (20) yield
\[
 h_g(x\mathbin{\pm}\delta)
 =h_g(x)\mathbin{\pm}\delta h_g'(x)
   +\frac{\delta^2}{2}h_g''(x)+\varepsilon_\pm(x),
 \tag{25}
\]
where
\[
 |\varepsilon_\pm(x)|
 \leq\frac{\delta^3C_2}{6}
       \sup_{|u-x|\leq\delta}(1+u^2)
 \leq\frac{\delta^3C_2}{2}(1+x^2).
 \tag{26}
\]
Substituting (22)--(26) into the scaled lattice generator gives
\[
 G_{1,N}h_g(x)
 =b_g(x)h_g'(x)+qh_g''(x)
  +\frac\delta2r_g^N(x)h_g''(x)+R_N(x),
 \tag{27}
\]
with
\[
 |R_N(x)|
 \leq\{B_N(x)+D_N^-(x)\}
       \max\{|\varepsilon_+(x)|,|\varepsilon_-(x)|\}
 \leq\frac{3CC_2}{2}\delta(1+x^2).
 \tag{28}
\]
Since \((1+|x|)^2\leq2(1+x^2)\), equations (18), (24), (27), and the definition of \(\mathcal L_g\) imply the pointwise, compact-uniform bound
\[
 |(G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_g)h_g(x)|
 \leq K_1\delta(1+x^2),
 \qquad
 K_1:=C_rC_1+\frac{3CC_2}{2}.
 \tag{29}
\]
Notice also that \(g=(M_N-Na)/\sqrt N\) is itself the lattice point corresponding to \(k=M_N\).  Thus a lattice edge can only remain on one smooth branch or have the kink as an endpoint.  Even without using this alignment, the absolute-continuity argument preceding (21) proves (25)--(29) for a genuinely crossing interval.

It remains to average (29) under the finite stationary law.  Applying the finite-state generator to \(x^2\) and using (22)--(23) gives exactly
\[
 G_{1,N}x^2=2xb_g(x)+2q+\delta r_g^N(x).
 \tag{30}
\]
By (2), (3), (6), and the sharper direct bound
\[
 |r_g^N(x)|\leq2C|x|+C\overline G,
 \tag{31}
\]
we have
\[
 G_{1,N}x^2
 \leq-2dx^2+L|x|+2C+C\overline G,
 \qquad L:=2C(\overline G+1).
 \tag{32}
\]
Young's inequality \(L|x|\leq dx^2+L^2/(4d)\), together with \(d\geq2c\), yields
\[
 G_{1,N}x^2\leq-dx^2+C_6,
 \qquad C_6:=2C+C\overline G+\frac{L^2}{8c}.
 \tag{33}
\]
The law \(\rho_{1,N}\) is stationary by definition and the treatment chain has the stated generator, so finite support permits termwise summation and gives \(\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}G_{1,N}x^2=0\).  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}X_{1,N}^2
 \leq\frac{C_6}{d}\leq\frac{C_6}{2c}.
 \tag{34}
\]
Taking stationary expectations in (29), using the lattice restriction \(h_{1,N}=h_g|_{E_{1,N}}\), and applying (34) proves
\[
 \mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}
 \left|\{G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_{\gamma_N}\}
 h_{1,N}(X_{1,N})\right|
 \leq K_1\left(1+\frac{C_6}{2c}\right)N^{-1/2}.
 \tag{35}
\]
Thus the required choice
\[
 K_{\mathrm{res}}=K_1\left(1+\frac{C_6}{2c}\right)
 \tag{36}
\]
is finite and depends only on \((c,C,G)\).  Since every bound before taking the supremum is uniform over \(p\in\mathcal P\) and \(|\gamma|\leq G\), equation (35) proves the asserted supremum inequality.

The estimate has the required centering consequence.  Stationarity gives \(\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}G_{1,N}h_{1,N}=0\), while the Poisson equation gives \(-\mathcal L_g h_g=x-m_g\).  Hence
\[
 \left|\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}X_{1,N}-m_{\gamma_N}\right|
 =\left|\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}
   [(G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_{\gamma_N})h_{1,N}(X_{1,N})]\right|
 \leq K_{\mathrm{res}}N^{-1/2}.
 \tag{37}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 \left|\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}\frac{K_{1,N}}N
 -\left\{a(p)+\frac{m_{\gamma_N}}{\sqrt N}\right\}\right|
 \leq\frac{K_{\mathrm{res}}}{N}.
 \tag{38}
\]
This proves the order required for diffusion fitted centering without assuming it.

As an ancillary early-kill stress test, not used in the proof, take \(c=1/2\), \(C=2\), and \(G=2\), for which the stated formula gives \(N_0=600\).  We evaluated the stationary weights from the exact product
\[
 \rho_{1,N}(k)\ \propto\
 \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}
 \frac{\lambda(N-j)}{\tau(j+1)+\nu\min\{j+1,M_N\}}
 \tag{39}
\]
at all eight corners of the rate box, at thirty-nine nominal offsets between \(-1.9\) and \(1.9\), and at ceiling offsets \(0,0.11,0.37,0.63,0.89\).  Analytic piecewise-Gaussian formulas for \(h_g'\), integrated on each lattice edge by twenty-point Gauss--Legendre quadrature, gave maxima of \(\sqrt N\,\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}|(G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_g)h_g|\) equal to \(0.0484345\), \(0.0479274\), and \(0.0475845\) at \(N=600,1200,2400\), respectively.  The worst corner was \((\lambda,\tau,\nu)=(1/2,1/2,2)\) near \(g=-0.2\).  This finite computation is consistent with (35), while (1)--(36), rather than the computation, certify every corner and ceiling phase.

proofs.proof_tex:
All probabilities and expectations in this proof are under a member of \(\mathcal M\).  In particular, the two chains start in their invariant laws and are independent by Definition \(\mathrm{model\mbox{-}class}\).  Write
\[
 f_{\ell,N}(x)=x-\mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}X_{\ell,N},
 \qquad -G_{\ell,N}u_{\ell,N}=f_{\ell,N},
 \qquad \mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}u_{\ell,N}=0.
\]
These Poisson solutions exist and have the edge and moment bounds asserted by Lemma \(\mathrm{finite\mbox{-}chain\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}controls}\).  Dynkin's formula gives the square-integrable martingales
\[
 M_{\ell,N}(t)=u_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(t))-u_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(0))
 -\int_0^tG_{\ell,N}u_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(s))\,ds
\]
and hence the exact identity
\[
 \int_0^{T_N}f_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(t))\,dt
 =M_{\ell,N}(T_N)-
 \{u_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(T_N))-u_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(0))\}.       \tag{1}
\]
The edge bound in that lemma makes \(u_{\ell,N}\) uniformly \(d^{-1}\)-Lipschitz on its scaled lattice.  Stationary centering of \(u_{\ell,N}\), followed by the uniform second-moment bound for \(X_{\ell,N}\), therefore gives
\[
 \sup_{N,p,\gamma,\ell}\mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}u_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N})^2<\infty. \tag{2}
\]
Since \(T_N\to\infty\), stationarity, (1), and (2) imply, uniformly in the parameter box,
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widehat\theta_N-\theta_N)
 =T_N^{-1/2}\{M_{0,N}(T_N)-M_{1,N}(T_N)\}+o_{\mathbb P}(1).       \tag{3}
\]

Define the compensated marked counts
\[
 U_{\lambda,N}=C_\lambda-\lambda E_\lambda,
 \qquad U_{\tau,N}=C_\tau-\tau E_\tau,
 \qquad U_{\nu,N}=C_\nu-\nu E_\nu.                              \tag{4}
\]
The generator assumptions identify the intensities in (4), and the marked-history assumption makes recoveries of the two types distinguishable.  Thus these are pairwise orthogonal square-integrable martingales with predictable brackets
\[
 \langle U_{\lambda,N}\rangle=\lambda E_\lambda,
 \qquad \langle U_{\tau,N}\rangle=\tau E_\tau,
 \qquad \langle U_{\nu,N}\rangle=\nu E_\nu.                     \tag{5}
\]
Put
\[
 s_\lambda=2-a_0-a,
 \qquad s_\tau=a_0+a,
 \qquad s_\nu=a.
\]
The stationary control mean is \(Na_0\).  The invariant-law convergence in Theorem \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\), together with uniform integrability from the moment bounds, gives \(N^{-1}\mathbb E K_{1,N}\to a\) uniformly.  The time-average conclusion of Lemma \(\mathrm{finite\mbox{-}chain\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}controls}\) then yields
\[
 \frac{1}{NT_N}(E_\lambda,E_\tau,E_\nu)
 \longrightarrow(s_\lambda,s_\tau,s_\nu)
 \quad\hbox{uniformly in probability}.                           \tag{6}
\]
Compact positivity implies \(\inf_{p\in\mathcal P}\min_j s_j>0\).  Consequently the prescribed fallbacks and clipping are inactive with probability tending to one uniformly, and, componentwise,
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widehat p_j-p_j)
 =\frac{U_{j,N}/\sqrt{NT_N}}{E_j/(NT_N)}
 =\frac{U_{j,N}}{s_j\sqrt{NT_N}}+o_{\mathbb P}(1).               \tag{7}
\]

We next calculate the entire limiting predictable bracket before invoking any limit theorem.  Define the four-dimensional martingale
\[
 \mathcal Z_N(t)=\left(
 \frac{M_{0,N}(t)-M_{1,N}(t)}{\sqrt{T_N}},
 \frac{U_{\lambda,N}(t)}{s_\lambda\sqrt{NT_N}},
 \frac{U_{\tau,N}(t)}{s_\tau\sqrt{NT_N}},
 \frac{U_{\nu,N}(t)}{s_\nu\sqrt{NT_N}}
 \right)^{\mathsf T}.                                           \tag{8}
\]
The stationary Poisson-energy identity and arm independence give
\[
 \langle\mathcal Z_N^{(1)}\rangle(T_N)
 =V_{0,N}+V_{1,N}+o_{\mathbb P}(1)
 \longrightarrow V_0+V_\gamma=V,                               \tag{9}
\]
where the last convergence is Theorem \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\), and the time-average replacement is supplied by the final assertion of Lemma \(\mathrm{finite\mbox{-}chain\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}controls}\).  Equations (5)--(6) give the lower diagonal block
\[
 \operatorname{diag}\left\{\frac{\lambda}{s_\lambda},
 \frac{\tau}{s_\tau},\frac{\nu}{s_\nu}\right\}=\Gamma.       \tag{10}
\]

For completeness, the cross bracket can be read event by event.  On an upward control edge, the scaled Poisson increment has stationary edge average tending to \(d^{-1}\); on an upward treatment edge it has average tending to \(H\).  Downward edges have the corresponding negatives after the natural index shift.  Because the occupation coordinate in (8) is \(M_{0,N}-M_{1,N}\), the un-divided limiting cross-bracket rates with the three count martingales are
\[
 \begin{split}
 c_\lambda
 &=\lambda\{(1-a_0)/d-(1-a)H\}=\lambda A_\lambda,\\
 c_\tau
 &=\tau\{-a_0/d+aH\}=\tau A_\tau,\\
 c_\nu
 &=\nu aH=\nu A_\nu.
 \end{split}                                                     \tag{11}
\]
Here the factors \(1-a_0,a_0,1-a,a\) are the limiting normalized at-risk occupations, and every edge-average limit is exactly the one stated in Lemma \(\mathrm{finite\mbox{-}chain\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}controls}\).  Dividing the three entries in (11) by \(s_\lambda,s_\tau,s_\nu\), as in (8), gives \(A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma\).  Combining (9)--(11),
\[
 \langle\mathcal Z_N\rangle(T_N)
 \longrightarrow
 \Sigma:=\begin{pmatrix}V&A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma\\
                          \Gamma A&\Gamma\end{pmatrix}
 \quad\hbox{uniformly in probability}.                          \tag{12}
\]

We derive the Gaussian conclusion from the primitive jump and bracket conditions.  The Poisson edge bound implies that an occupation-martingale jump in (8) is at most \(d^{-1}/\sqrt{NT_N}\).  A normalized count jump is at most
\(\{\min_j s_j\}^{-1}/\sqrt{NT_N}\).  Hence, for each fixed \(t\in\mathbb R^4\), the scalar martingale \(L_N=t^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Z_N\) has maximal jump bounded by a deterministic \(\varepsilon_N\to0\), uniformly in the parameter box, and
\[
 \langle L_N\rangle(T_N)\longrightarrow t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma t. \tag{13}
\]
To see directly that (13) implies the required scalar central limit theorem here, stop when the bracket first exceeds a fixed \(R>t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma t+1\).  The jump formula for the exponential, together with
\[
 e^{iu}=1+iu-u^2/2+r(u),\qquad |r(u)|\leq |u|^3/6,               \tag{14}
\]
shows, after compensating the jumps, that
\[
 \left|\mathbb E\exp\left\{iL_N+\frac12\langle L_N\rangle\right\}-1\right|
 \leq C_{t,R}\varepsilon_N R                                  \tag{15}
\]
for the stopped martingale and stopped bracket.  Indeed, every cubic remainder is at most \(\varepsilon_N\) times its quadratic term, and the predictable sum of the quadratic terms is the stopped bracket; the exponential factor is bounded because that bracket is at most \(R+o(1)\).  The right-hand side of (15) tends to zero.  By (13), the stopped bracket converges in probability to \(t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma t\), so bounded convergence in (15) gives the stopped characteristic-function limit \(\exp\{-t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma t/2\}\).  The probability of stopping tends to zero, again by (13).  Thus
\[
 \mathbb E\exp\{it^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Z_N(T_N)\}
 \longrightarrow \exp\{-t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma t/2\}.             \tag{16}
\]
This argument also covers \(t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma t=0\).  The Cram\'er--Wold criterion applied to (16), followed by (3) and (7), proves the displayed joint Gaussian law.

All constants used above are uniform over the compact rate and staffing set.  More explicitly, if uniform convergence failed, a failing parameter sequence would have a convergent subsequence; (2), (6), (9), (11), and the jump bounds hold on that subsequence with the same constants, while the Gaussian integrals defining \(V,H,A,\Gamma\) vary continuously.  Equations (12)--(16) would then contradict the alleged failure.  This proves the asserted uniformity.

It remains to studentize.  Equation (7) implies \(\widehat p-p=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly, and
\[
 \widehat\gamma_N-\gamma_N
 =-\sqrt N\{a(\widehat p)-a(p)\}=O_{\mathbb P}(T_N^{-1/2}),
 \qquad 0\leq\gamma_N-\gamma<N^{-1/2}.                           \tag{17}
\]
The explicit Gaussian integrals defining \(V\) are continuous on every compact positive-rate and bounded-staffing set.  Moreover
\(V\geq V_0=2\lambda\tau/d^3\), whose infimum on \(\mathcal P\) is positive.  Therefore \(\widehat V/V\to1\) uniformly in probability.  Studentization of the first coordinate and continuity of the standard normal distribution function give
\[
 \sup_{p\in\mathcal P,\,|\gamma|\leq G}
 \left|\mathbb P_{p,\gamma}\{\theta_N\in I_{\mathrm{emp}}\}-(1-\alpha)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
Only exact prelimit martingales on \([0,T_N]\) were used; no path approximation on a growing interval and no upper relation between \(T_N\) and \(N\) entered the proof.  Finally, Lemma \(\mathrm{boutilier\mbox{-}anchor\mbox{-}scope}\) gives precisely the comparison in the last two sentences of the theorem and supplies no class-transfer premise.

Work over \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{fit}}\).  Its primitive sampling and dynamics conditions are the same as those used in Theorem \(\mathrm{uniform\mbox{-}joint\mbox{-}law}\), and it imposes only the joint divergences \(N,T_N\to\infty\).  Denote
\[
 S_N=\sqrt{NT_N}(\widehat\theta_N-\theta_N),
 \qquad R_N=\sqrt{NT_N}(\widehat p-p).
\]
The joint theorem gives, uniformly,
\[
 (S_N,R_N)\Rightarrow(S,R),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(S)=V,quad
 \operatorname{Var}(R)=\Gamma,quad
 \operatorname{Cov}(R,S)=\Gamma A,                              \tag{17}
\]
and in particular \(\widehat p-p=O_{\mathbb P}((NT_N)^{-1/2})\).

The product weights in Definition \(\mathrm{fitted\mbox{-}center}\) are the detailed-balance weights of the two finite birth--death generators.  Hence Lemma \(\mathrm{exact\mbox{-}fixed\mbox{-}capacity\mbox{-}derivative}\) gives
\(\vartheta_N(p;M_N)=\theta_N\).  On the event that the clipped estimator lies in \([c/2,2C]^3\), Taylor's formula is applied to \(p'\mapsto\vartheta_N(p';M_N)\) while holding the implemented integer \(M_N\) fixed.  The same lemma yields
\[
 \begin{split}
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widetilde\theta_N-\theta_N)
 &=\nabla_{p'}\vartheta_N(p';M_N)|_{p'=p}^{\mathsf T}R_N+\mathcal R_N,\\
 |\mathcal R_N|
 &\leq \frac{C_*}{2}\sqrt{NT_N}\sqrt N\,\|\widehat p-p\|^2
 =O_{\mathbb P}(T_N^{-1/2})=o_{\mathbb P}(1).                   
 \end{split}                                                     \tag{18}
\]
Uniform consistency from (17) and the compact interior rate bounds show that clipping or fallback has probability tending to zero uniformly.  The derivative convergence in that lemma therefore turns (18) into
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widetilde\theta_N-\theta_N)
 =A^{\mathsf T}R_N+o_{\mathbb P}(1)
 \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma A).               \tag{19}
\]
No comparison between \(T_N\) and \(N\) occurs in (18); only \(T_N\to\infty\) is required.

The formula for the derivative limit can also be checked componentwise.  Since
\[
 \nabla a_0=((1-a_0)/d,-a_0/d,0)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad
 D\nabla a=(1-a,-a,-a)^{\mathsf T},
\]
one has
\[
 \nabla a_0-DH\nabla a
 =((1-a_0)/d-(1-a)H,-a_0/d+aH,aH)^{\mathsf T}=A.                \tag{20}
\]
Thus (19) has variance \(Q=A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma A\), exactly as stated.

Subtracting (19) from the first coordinate in (17) gives
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\widehat\theta_N-\widetilde\theta_N)
 \Rightarrow S-A^{\mathsf T}R.                                  \tag{21}
\]
Using all three covariance identities in (17),
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(S-A^{\mathsf T}R)
 =V+A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma A-2A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma A
 =V-A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma A=W.                                  \tag{22}
\]
In particular, (22) also proves \(W\geq0\), because it is the variance of the displayed Gaussian linear combination.

For Wald coverage, Theorem \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\) gives \(H\geq1/D\).  Since the service coordinate is \(A_\nu=aH\) and \(\Gamma_{\nu\nu}=\nu/a\),
\[
 Q=A^{\mathsf T}\Gamma A\geq\frac{\nu}{a}(aH)^2=\nu aH^2.     \tag{23}
\]
Compact positive rate bounds make the right-hand side uniformly positive.  Moreover,
\[
 \widehat\gamma_N-\gamma_N
 =-\sqrt N\{a(\widehat p)-a(p)\}=O_{\mathbb P}(T_N^{-1/2}),
 \qquad 0\leq\gamma_N-\gamma<N^{-1/2}.                          \tag{24}
\]
The explicit integral defining \(H\), and hence \(A\) and \(Q\), is continuous on compact positive-rate and bounded-staffing sets.  Equations (17), (23), and (24) thus imply
\(\widehat Q/Q\to1\) uniformly in probability.  Dividing (19) by \(\sqrt{\widehat Q}\), using the fixed quantile supplied by \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and applying continuity of the standard normal distribution function proves
\[
 \sup_{p\in\mathcal P,\,|\gamma|\leq G}
 \left|\mathbb P_{p,\gamma}\{\theta_N\in I_{\mathrm{fit}}\}-(1-\alpha)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
Together, (19)--(24) prove every assertion, including the fixed-staffing correction and the absence of an upper horizon restriction.

Put \(\delta=N^{-1/2}\) and \(g=\gamma_N\).  The ceiling identity gives
\(0\leq g-\gamma<\delta\), so \(|g|\leq G+1\).  All constants below may therefore be chosen uniformly over the compact positive rate box and the enlarged staffing interval \([-G-1,G+1]\).  Write \(h_g=h_{p,g}\) and
\[
 b_g(x)=-dx-\nu\min\{x,g\}.
\]
By Theorem \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\),
\[
 \frac1D\leq h_g'(x)\leq\frac1d,                               \tag{25}
\]
and the Poisson equation in Definition \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\) is
\[
 qh_g''(x)=-(x-m_g)-b_g(x)h_g'(x).                              \tag{26}
\]

We first establish derivative envelopes, including at the kink.  The explicit piecewise-Gaussian density has Gaussian tails uniformly on the enlarged compact parameter set, so the stationary identity for \(x^2\) follows by applying the generator identity first to smooth compactly supported truncations and then passing to the limit.  Since
\[
 \mathcal L_gx^2=2xb_g(x)+2q
 =-2dx^2-2\nu x\min\{x,g\}+2q
\]
and
\(x\min\{x,g\}\geq-(G+1)|x|\), Young's inequality gives constants \(c_1,c_2<\infty\), depending only on \((c,C,G)\), such that
\[
 0=\int\mathcal L_gx^2\,\pi_g(x)\,dx
 \leq-c_1\int x^2\pi_g(x)\,dx+c_2.                            \tag{27}
\]
Thus \(\sup_{p,g}\int x^2\pi_g(x)\,dx<\infty\), and Cauchy--Schwarz gives \(\sup_{p,g}|m_g|<\infty\).  The quantities \(q^{-1}\), \(d\), \(D\), and \(\nu\) are uniformly bounded on the rate box.  Therefore (25)--(26) imply
\[
 |h_g''(x)|\leq C_1(1+|x|).                                    \tag{28}
\]
On each open side of \(g\), differentiation of (26) gives
\[
 qh_g'''(x)=-1-b_g'(x)h_g'(x)-b_g(x)h_g''(x),                  \tag{29}
\]
where \(b_g'=-D\) on the left and \(b_g'=-d\) on the right.  Equations (25), (28), and (29) yield
\[
 |h_g'''(x)|\leq C_2(1+x^2),\qquad x\neq g.                    \tag{30}
\]
The drift \(b_g\) is continuous at \(g\), as are \(h_g'\) and the right-hand side of (26).  Hence \(h_g''\) is continuous at \(g\).  Since it is continuously differentiable on either side with the locally bounded derivative (30), \(h_g''\) is locally absolutely continuous across \(g\).  Taylor's formula with integral remainder is consequently valid even when the increment interval contains the kink; the value of \(h_g'''\) at the single point \(g\) is immaterial.

At \(x=(k-Na)/\sqrt N\), let
\[
 B_N(x)=\lambda(N-k),
 \qquad D_N(x)=\tau k+\nu\min\{k,M_N\},
\]
with the unavailable endpoint rate equal to zero.  Because
\(k=Na+\sqrt N x\), \(M_N=Na+\sqrt N g\), and \(a=\lambda/D\), direct algebra gives at every lattice state, including both endpoints,
\[
 \delta\{B_N(x)-D_N(x)\}=b_g(x),                               \tag{31}
\]
and
\[
 \frac{\delta^2}{2}\{B_N(x)+D_N(x)\}
 =q+\frac\delta2\{(\tau-\lambda)x+\nu\min(x,g)\}.             \tag{32}
\]
Taylor expansion of the two available lattice increments, using the integral remainder justified above, now gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 G_{1,N}h_g(x)
 &=b_g(x)h_g'(x)
 +\left[q+\frac\delta2\{(\tau-\lambda)x+\nu\min(x,g)\}\right]h_g''(x)
 +R_N(x),\\
 |R_N(x)|
 &\leq\frac{\delta^3}{6}\{B_N(x)+D_N(x)\}
 \mathop{\operatorname{ess\,sup}}_{|u-x|\leq\delta}|h_g'''(u)|.
 \end{split}                                                     \tag{33}
\]
The rate bounds imply \(B_N+D_N\leq3CN\).  From (30),
\[
 |R_N(x)|\leq C_3\delta(1+x^2).                                \tag{34}
\]
Also \(|\min(x,g)|\leq |x|+G+1\), so (28) bounds the extra second-derivative term in (33) by \(C_4\delta(1+x^2)\).  Subtracting
\(\mathcal L_gh_g=b_gh_g'+qh_g''\) proves the pointwise, kink-inclusive estimate
\[
 |(G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_g)h_g(x)|
 \leq C_5\delta(1+x^2)                                         \tag{35}
\]
at every \(x\in E_{1,N}\).

It remains only to average (35) under the exact stationary law.  Applying (31)--(32) to the function \(x^2\) gives the exact finite-chain identity
\[
 G_{1,N}x^2
 =2xb_g(x)+2q+delta\{(\tau-\lambda)x+\nu\min(x,g)\}.          \tag{36}
\]
Using again \(x\min(x,g)\geq-(G+1)|x|\), \(|\min(x,g)|\leq|x|+G+1\), \(\delta\leq1\), and Young's inequality, there is a uniform constant \(C_6\) such that
\[
 G_{1,N}x^2\leq-dx^2+C_6.                                      \tag{37}
\]
The state space is finite, and the treatment chain starts in \(\rho_{1,N}\); hence stationarity gives \(\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}G_{1,N}X_{1,N}^2=0\).  It follows from (37) that
\[
 \sup_{N,p,\gamma}\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}X_{1,N}^2\leq C_6/d. \tag{38}
\]
Taking expectations in (35) and using (38) proves the theorem with
\(K_{\mathrm{res}}=C_5(1+C_6/d)\), enlarged if necessary to replace \(d\) by its compact-set lower bound.

The calculation also supplies the requested boundary and ceiling stress test.  The exact birth--death product law is
\[
 \rho_{1,N}(k)=Z_N^{-1}\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}
 \frac{\lambda(N-j)}{\tau(j+1)+\nu\min\{j+1,M_N\}},            \tag{39}
\]
with the empty product equal to one.  Estimate (35) holds before multiplication by any weight in (39), with the same constant at all asymmetric corners of the compact rate box and for every value of the ceiling phase \(g-\gamma\in[0,\delta)\).  Thus no stationary product weighting can create a nonvanishing scaled residual.  As the smallest algebraic interior-capacity check, take \(N=2\) and \(M_N=1\): the states \(k=0,1,2\) are respectively the left endpoint, the kink state, and the right endpoint, and (31)--(35) cover every one of the four directed available transitions.  For larger \(N\), a jump crossing \(g\) is already covered by the absolute-continuity remainder in (33).

Finally, stationarity and the diffusion Poisson equation show the useful centering consequence
\[
 \begin{split}
 \left|\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}X_{1,N}-m_g\right|
 &=\left|\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}}
 \{(G_{1,N}-\mathcal L_g)h_g\}(X_{1,N})\right|\\
 &\leq K_{\mathrm{res}}N^{-1/2}.                               
 \end{split}                                                     \tag{40}
\]
This also rules out the early-kill alternative of an order-one residual at a corner, endpoint, kink-crossing edge, or ceiling phase.

Let \(p'\in[c/2,2C]^3\), let \(1\leq M\leq N-1\), and set
\[
 g'=(M-Na(p'))/\sqrt N.
\]
The control invariant mean is exactly \(a_0(p')\).  By the definition of the scaled treatment state, the treatment invariant mean divided by \(N\) is
\[
 a(p')+N^{-1/2}\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}^{p',M}}X_{1,N}^{p',M}.
\]
Consequently the exact product-law effect and its diffusion approximation differ by
\[
 \vartheta_N(p';M)-\{a_0(p')-a(p')-N^{-1/2}m_{p',g'}\}
 =-N^{-1/2}\{\mathbb E_{\rho_{1,N}^{p',M}}X_{1,N}^{p',M}-m_{p',g'}\}. \tag{41}
\]

Theorem \(\mathrm{kink\mbox{-}residual\mbox{-}bound}\), and specifically its centering consequence (40), applies with new fixed compact constants to the rate box \([c/2,2C]^3\) and any fixed enlarged staffing window.  It follows from (41) that, uniformly whenever \(|g'|\leq G+1\) and for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\[
 \left|\vartheta_N(p';M)-\{a_0(p')-a(p')-N^{-1/2}m_{p',g'}\}\right|
 \leq K N^{-1}.                                                  \tag{42}
\]

Under the rate-score coordinate of Theorem \(\mathrm{uniform\mbox{-}joint\mbox{-}law}\),
\[
 \widehat p-p=O_{\mathbb P}((NT_N)^{-1/2})
\]
uniformly.  Smoothness of \(a\) on the compact positive rate box therefore gives
\[
 \widehat\gamma_N-\gamma_N
 =-\sqrt N\{a(\widehat p)-a(p)\}
 =O_{\mathbb P}(T_N^{-1/2}),
 \qquad 0\leq\gamma_N-\gamma<N^{-1/2}.                          \tag{43}
\]
Since \(T_N\to\infty\), (43) implies that the event
\(\widehat p\in[c/2,2C]^3\) and \(|\widehat\gamma_N|\leq G+1\) has probability tending to one uniformly.  On this event take \(p'=\widehat p\) and \(M=M_N\) in (42).  Definitions \(\mathrm{fitted\mbox{-}center}\) then give
\[
 \overline\theta_N-\widetilde\theta_N=O_{\mathbb P}(N^{-1})
 \quad\hbox{uniformly}.                                         \tag{44}
\]
Under the additional primitive condition \(T_N/N\to0\),
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\overline\theta_N-\widetilde\theta_N)
 =O_{\mathbb P}(\sqrt{T_N/N})=o_{\mathbb P}(1).                 \tag{45}
\]
Theorem \(\mathrm{fitted\mbox{-}center\mbox{-}wald}\) gives
\(\sqrt{NT_N}(\widetilde\theta_N-\theta_N)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,Q)\) and \(\widehat Q/Q\to1\) uniformly, with \(Q\) bounded away from zero.  Equations (44)--(45) and Slutsky's argument therefore give
\[
 \sqrt{NT_N}(\overline\theta_N-\theta_N)
 \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,Q).
\]
Studentization by \(\widehat Q\), the assumption \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and continuity of the standard normal distribution function yield
\[
 \sup_{p\in\mathcal P,\,|\gamma|\leq G}
 \left|\mathbb P_{p,\gamma}\{\theta_N\in I_{\mathrm{diff}}\}-(1-\alpha)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus (44) proves the stated \(O_{\mathbb P}(N^{-1})\) approximation, and (45) identifies exactly where, and only where, the additional horizon restriction is used.

Write \(p=(\lambda,\tau,\nu)^{\mathsf T}\), and temporarily write \(\eta\) for the staffing argument of the objective.  We give an explicit construction of the oracle and prove each part of its contract.

First extract rational bounds from one entry of the supplied name \(\mathfrak r\).  The positivity and interior certificates in Definition \(\mathrm{input\mbox{-}name}\), together with Assumptions \(\mathrm{rate\mbox{-}membership}\), \(\mathrm{staffing\mbox{-}cost\mbox{-}positive}\), \(\mathrm{information\mbox{-}cost\mbox{-}positive}\), and \(\mathrm{test\mbox{-}size}\), permit finite rational choices
\[
 0<r_-\leq \lambda,\tau,\nu\leq r_+,
 \quad 0<c_M\leq c_M^+,
 \quad 0<c_I\leq c_I^+,
 \quad 0<\alpha_-\leq\alpha\leq\alpha_+<1,
 \quad 0\leq G\leq g_+.
\]
For example, one may take the minimum of the certified positive lower endpoints and the maximum of the upper endpoints of that entry.  Thus this extraction uses only comparisons of rational numbers.  Put
\[
 d_*=2r_-,\qquad
 q_-={2r_-^2\over 3r_+},\qquad
 q^*={2r_+^2\over 3r_-},\qquad
 v_*={r_-^2\over4r_+^3}.
\]
The definitions of \(d,q,V_0\) give, throughout this rational box,
\[
 d\geq d_*,\qquad q_-\leq q\leq q^*,\qquad
 V_0={2\lambda\tau\over(\lambda+\tau)^3}\geq v_*>0.                                      \tag{1}
\]

We next derive a computable Lipschitz bound in \(\eta\).  Define
\[
 \Psi_\eta(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 {D x^2\over2q},&x\leq\eta,\\[2mm]
 {d x^2\over2q}+{\nu\eta x\over q}-{\nu\eta^2\over2q},&x>\eta,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad w_\eta(x)=\exp\{-\Psi_\eta(x)\},
 \qquad Z_\eta=\int_{\mathbb R}w_\eta(x)\,dx.                                      \tag{2}
\]
The two values and the two first derivatives in \(x\) agree at \(x=\eta\).  Hence (2) has no boundary atom at the moving kink.  Direct differentiation shows
\[
 \Psi_\eta'(x)={d x+\nu\min\{x,\eta\}\over q},
 \qquad
 \partial_\eta\Psi_\eta(x)=s_\eta(x):={\nu\over q}(x-\eta)_+.                    \tag{3}
\]
Consequently the normalized density in (2) is exactly \(\pi_\eta=w_\eta/Z_\eta\) from the frozen definition of \(\pi_\gamma\).  If
\[
 m_\eta={1\over Z_\eta}\int_{\mathbb R}xw_\eta(x)\,dx,
 \qquad
 T_\eta(x)=\int_x^\infty (u-m_\eta)w_\eta(u)\,du,
\]
then the flux formula in Definition \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\) yields
\[
 y_\eta(x):=h_\eta'(x)={T_\eta(x)\over q w_\eta(x)},
 \qquad
 V_\eta={2\over qZ_\eta}\int_{\mathbb R}{T_\eta(x)^2\over w_\eta(x)}\,dx.          \tag{4}
\]
This is already a one-dimensional quadrature formula, and all of its inner quantities have explicit Gaussian forms.  To make the later certificate completely concrete, set
\[
 \sigma_L=\sqrt{q/D},\qquad \sigma_R=\sqrt{q/d},\qquad
 \mu_R=-{\nu\eta\over d},\qquad
 C_\eta=\exp\!\left({\nu D\eta^2\over2dq}\right),
\]
and set
\[
 E(t)=e^{-t^2/2},\qquad
 F(t)=\int_{-\infty}^t e^{-u^2/2}\,du=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\Phi(t),
 \qquad \overline F(t)=\sqrt{2\pi}-F(t).
\]
With \(t_L=\eta/\sigma_L\) and \(t_R=(\eta-\mu_R)/\sigma_R\), direct changes of variable and one integration by parts give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Z_\eta&=\sigma_LF(t_L)+C_\eta\sigma_R\overline F(t_R),\\
 Z_\eta m_\eta
 &=-\sigma_L^2E(t_L)
   +C_\eta\{\mu_R\sigma_R\overline F(t_R)+\sigma_R^2E(t_R)\}.
 \end{aligned}                                                                       \tag{4a}
\]
Moreover, the centering identity \(\int_{\mathbb R}(u-m_\eta)w_\eta(u)\,du=0\) gives the cancellation-stable flux formulas
\[
 T_\eta(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 \sigma_L^2E(x/\sigma_L)+m_\eta\sigma_LF(x/\sigma_L),&x\leq\eta,\\[1mm]
 C_\eta\bigl[(\mu_R-m_\eta)\sigma_R\overline F((x-\mu_R)/\sigma_R)
       +\sigma_R^2E((x-\mu_R)/\sigma_R)\bigr],&x>\eta.
 \end{cases}                                                                         \tag{4b}
\]
Thus evaluating (4) requires only rational interval evaluations of exponential, square root, \(\Phi\), and one final proper quadrature after a certified tail truncation.
Theorem \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\) gives the uniform pointwise bounds
\[
 {1\over D}\leq y_\eta(x)\leq {1\over d}.                                          \tag{5}
\]

Let \(X\) have density \(\pi_\eta\).  From (3), differentiation under the integral in (2) gives
\[
 m_\eta'=-\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_\eta}\{X,s_\eta(X)\}.                            \tag{6}
\]
This differentiation is justified by a quadratic Gaussian envelope: \(\Psi_\eta\) is \(d/q\)-strongly convex, uniformly on each side of the kink, and is continuously differentiable at the kink.  The same envelope justifies all differentiations below.

We record bounds needed in (6).  By reversibility, the Poisson equation and integration by parts give
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{\pi_\eta}(X)
 =\int (x-m_\eta)(-\mathcal L_\eta h_\eta)(x)\pi_\eta(x)\,dx
 =q\int y_\eta(x)\pi_\eta(x)\,dx
 \leq {q\over d},                                                                    \tag{7}
\]
where the last inequality is (5).  For an independent copy \(X'\), the covariance identity and the \(\nu/q\)-Lipschitz property of \(s_\eta\) imply
\[
 \left|\operatorname{Cov}\{X,s_\eta(X)\}\right|
 =\left|{1\over2}\mathbb E[(X-X')\{s_\eta(X)-s_\eta(X')\}]\right|
 \leq {\nu\over q}\operatorname{Var}(X)
 \leq {\nu\over d}.                                                                 \tag{8}
\]

Differentiate the first-order form of the Poisson equation,
\[
 qy_\eta'(x)-\{dx+\nu\min(x,\eta)\}y_\eta(x)=m_\eta-x.
\]
With \(z_\eta=\partial_\eta y_\eta\), equations (5), (6), and (8) give
\[
 qz_\eta'(x)-\{dx+\nu\min(x,\eta)\}z_\eta(x)
 =g_\eta(x):=m_\eta'+\nu\mathbf 1\{x>\eta\}y_\eta(x),
 \qquad \|g_\eta\|_\infty\leq {2\nu\over d}.                                    \tag{9}
\]
The flux integration-by-parts identity \(\operatorname{Cov}\{X,f(X)\}=q\mathbb E[y_\eta(X)f'(X)]\), first for smooth \(f\) and then by Lipschitz approximation, applied to \(f=s_\eta\) combines with (6) to give \(m_\eta'=-\nu\mathbb E[y_\eta(X)\mathbf 1\{X>\eta\}]\).  Hence \(\int g_\eta\pi_\eta=0\).  If \(\mu_\eta\) is the unique minimizer of \(\Psi_\eta\), strong convexity gives, for \(x\leq\mu_\eta\),
\[
 {\int_{-\infty}^x\pi_\eta(u)\,du\over\pi_\eta(x)}
 \leq\int_0^\infty e^{-dt^2/(2q)}\,dt,
\]
and gives the analogous right-tail inequality for \(x\geq\mu_\eta\).  Solving (9) by its integrating factor and using the smaller of these two tails therefore gives
\[
 \|z_\eta\|_\infty
 \leq {2\nu\over d}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2dq}}.                                         \tag{10}
\]
Notice that (9)--(10) also verify the kink case: the coefficient has a jump in its derivative only on a set of stationary measure zero, while (3) vanishes at the joining point, so no unaccounted moving-boundary term occurs.

The minimizer is explicit:
\[
 \mu_\eta=0\quad(\eta\geq0),
 \qquad
 \mu_\eta=-{\nu\eta\over d}\quad(\eta<0).                                          \tag{11}
\]
Integration of the derivative of \((x-\mu_\eta)e^{-\Psi_\eta(x)}\), followed by strong convexity, yields
\[
 1=\mathbb E[(X-\mu_\eta)\Psi_\eta'(X)]
 \geq {d\over q}\mathbb E[(X-\mu_\eta)^2].                                         \tag{12}
\]
It follows from (11)--(12), for \(|\eta|\leq G\), that
\[
 \mathbb E[(X-\eta)_+]
 \leq G\left(1+{\nu\over d}\right)+\sqrt{q/d}.                                    \tag{13}
\]

Since \(\partial_\eta\log\pi_\eta=-s_\eta+\mathbb E s_\eta\), differentiation of the energy in (4) gives the exact identity
\[
 V_\eta'
 =2q\,\mathbb E\left[2y_\eta z_\eta-
       \{s_\eta-\mathbb E s_\eta\}y_\eta^2\right].                               \tag{14}
\]
Using (5), (10), the nonnegativity of \(s_\eta\), and (13) in (14) proves
\[
 |V_\eta'|
 \leq {8\nu q\over d^2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2dq}}
 +{4\nu\over d^2}\left[G\left(1+{\nu\over d}\right)+\sqrt{q/d}\right].          \tag{15}
\]
All bounds remain finite at every asymmetric corner of the original rate box because \(q_->0\) and \(d_*>0\).

We now turn (15) into a rational certificate.  By finite searches over positive rationals choose \(s_1,s_2,s_0\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) such that
\[
 s_1^2>{2\over d_*q_-},\qquad
 s_2^2>{q^*\over d_*},\qquad
 s_0^2>{1\over v_*}.
\]
The first inequality is valid for the square root in (15) because \(\pi<4\).  Define the rational number
\[
 B_*={8r_+q^*\over d_*^2}s_1
 +{4r_+\over d_*^2}\left[g_+\left(1+{r_+\over d_*}\right)+s_2\right].               \tag{16}
\]
Choose an integer \(z^*>0\) with \((z^*)^2>2/\alpha_-\).  If \(Z\) is standard normal, Chebyshev's inequality, proved here by
\(\Pr(|Z|\geq z)\leq\mathbb E Z^2/z^2=1/z^2\), shows
\(1-\Phi(z^*)<\alpha_-/2\).  Hence \(0<z_\alpha<z^*\).  Equations (1), (15), and (16), followed by the ordinary chain rule, now give
\[
 \left|{\partial\over\partial\eta}J(p,\eta)\right|
 \leq c_M^+ + {c_I^+z^*B_*s_0\over2}.
\]
Thus the following is an explicit positive rational global modulus:
\[
 L_J=1+c_M^+ + {c_I^+z^*B_*s_0\over2}.                                               \tag{17}
\]
In particular, the mean-value theorem and (17) prove
\[
 |J(p,\eta)-J(p,\xi)|\leq L_J|\eta-\xi|,
 \qquad \eta,\xi\in[-G,G].                                                           \tag{18}
\]

For completeness, we next construct a finite, rationally checkable point evaluator; this is the part that turns the analytic formula into an objective oracle rather than assuming an oracle.  Given rational \(\eta\in[-g_+,g_+]\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\), the evaluator \(\mathsf E(\eta,k)=[e^-(\eta,k),e^+(\eta,k)]\) is produced as follows.

Use the two Gaussian pieces in (2), the moment formula and the flux-energy formula (4).  Multiplying \(w_\eta\) by \(e^{\Psi_\eta(\mu_\eta)}\) changes neither \(\pi_\eta\), \(m_\eta\), \(y_\eta\), nor \(V_\eta\).  For this rescaled weight, strong convexity and (11) give
\[
 0<\widetilde w_\eta(x)
 \leq \exp\left\{-{d_*\over2q^*}(x-\mu_\eta)^2\right\},
 \qquad |\mu_\eta|\leq {r_+g_+\over d_*}.                                          \tag{19}
\]
Choose a rational \(R>1+r_+g_+/d_*\).  The elementary integration-by-parts bounds
\[
 \int_a^\infty e^{-\kappa t^2/2}\,dt
 \leq {e^{-\kappa a^2/2}\over\kappa a},
 \qquad
 \int_a^\infty t e^{-\kappa t^2/2}\,dt
 ={e^{-\kappa a^2/2}\over\kappa},                                                    \tag{20}
\]
with \(\kappa=d_*/q^*\), give rationally certifiable tail enclosures for \(Z_\eta\) and its first moment after enclosing the exponential.  They tend to zero as \(R\to\infty\).  Independently, (5), (11), (12), and Markov's inequality give the energy-tail certificate
\[
 2q\,\mathbb E\!left[y_\eta(X)^2\mathbf 1\{|X|>R\}\right]
 \leq {2(q^*)^2\over d_*^3\{R-r_+g_+/d_*\}^2}.                                     \tag{21}
\]
Thus a finite integer search finds \(R\) for which every tail contribution requested by precision \(k\) is below any prescribed rational fraction of \(2^{-k}\).

On \([-R,R]\), split the interval at \(\eta\).  Compute intervals for \(Z_\eta\) and \(m_\eta\) from (4a), compute the flux on every cell from the appropriate branch of (4b), and enclose the final integral in (4) by upper and lower Darboux sums.  Exponentials are enclosed by range-reduced Taylor intervals and the occurrences of \(F\) and \(\overline F\) are enclosed through the certified normal integral (22) below.  Every denominator is certified away from zero: \(q\geq q_-\); either positive term in (4a) gives \(Z_\eta>0\); and continuity and positivity of \(w_\eta\) give a positive rational lower bound on \([-R,R]\).  The input box is refined from \(\mathfrak r\) until these lower bounds are exposed.  Inequality (21) is then added symmetrically to the truncated energy interval, so the result encloses the full integral.

These enclosures are finite and checkable using rational arithmetic.  More explicitly, for \(|u|\leq1\), the first \(n\) terms of the exponential series have a remainder bounded by \(3/(n+1)!\); repeated squaring after replacing an arbitrary bounded argument by \(u/2^j\) supplies a rational exponential interval.  Rational square-root intervals are obtained by bisection and comparison of squares.  The identity
\[
 \pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)
\]
follows by the tangent addition formula, and the alternating arctangent series supplies rational upper and lower bounds with the first omitted term as remainder.  Hence the normalizing constant used by \(\Phi\) also has finite rational witnesses.

For \(z_\alpha\), restrict to \([0,z^*]\).  Certified Darboux sums for
\[
 \Phi(z)={1\over2}+{1\over\sqrt{2\pi}}
                    \int_0^z e^{-t^2/2}\,dt                                          \tag{22}
\]
and refinements of the supplied interval for \(\alpha\) yield a certified bracket for the unique solution of \(\Phi(z)=1-\alpha/2\).  Termination is quantitative: on \([0,z^*]\),
\[
 \Phi'(z)\geq {e^{-(z^*)^2/2}\over\sqrt{2\pi}}>0,
\]
and a rational positive lower bound is obtained by the preceding exponential and square-root enclosures.  A rational grid of sufficiently small mesh, retaining exactly the cells whose certified \(\Phi\)-images meet the current interval for \(1-\alpha/2\), therefore has hull width at most the mesh plus the evaluation and input widths divided by that derivative lower bound.  Refining all three quantities gives any requested bracket width.

The preceding procedure terminates for the energy as well.  Indeed, (19)--(21) make the discarded tails arbitrarily small.  On the retained compact interval, each piece of every integrand is continuously differentiable with bounded derivative; the two pieces meet continuously at \(\eta\).  Therefore the difference of its upper and lower Darboux sums is bounded by its certified derivative bound times the mesh length.  The widths caused by the input name tend to zero because all displayed operations are rational operations, exponentials, square roots, and divisions by the positive lower bounds just exhibited.  Refining the input index, Taylor orders, \(R\), and the rational meshes must consequently produce a finite trace satisfying
\[
 J(p,\eta)\in\mathsf E(\eta,k),
 \qquad e^+(\eta,k)-e^-(\eta,k)\leq2^{-k}.                                           \tag{23}
\]
The trace consists of the chosen input index, \(R\), the two rational partitions, Taylor orders and remainder inequalities, denominator lower bounds, the tail inequalities (20)--(21), the quantile grid and (22), and the final interval-arithmetic expression.  A verifier checks only finitely many rational inequalities and integer factorials.  Thus (23) supplies the finite checkable evaluation witnesses demanded in the theorem.

It remains to assemble interval evaluations.  For a rational interval \(I=[a,b]\subseteq[-G,G]\), let
\[
 \eta_I={a+b\over2},\qquad \Delta_I=b-a,
 \qquad [e^-,e^+]=\mathsf E(\eta_I,m),
\]
and define rational endpoints
\[
 \underline J(I,m)=e^- -{L_J\Delta_I\over2},
 \qquad
 \overline J(I,m)=e^+ +{L_J\Delta_I\over2}.                                         \tag{24}
\]
For every \(\eta\in I\), (18), (23), and \(|\eta-\eta_I|\leq\Delta_I/2\) show
\[
 J(p,\eta)\in[\underline J(I,m),\overline J(I,m)].
\]
Moreover, (23)--(24) give the required explicit modulus,
\[
 \overline J(I,m)-\underline J(I,m)
 \leq L_J\operatorname{diam}(I)+2^{-m}.                                               \tag{25}
\]
If \(I\) is a point interval, \(\Delta_I=0\), so its returned width is at most \(2^{-m}\).  Equations (17), (23), and (24), together with their finite rational traces, therefore construct \((L_J,\mathfrak O)\) from the supplied input name and verify every enclosure, width, and point-width clause of Definition \(\mathrm{interval\mbox{-}oracle}\).  Oracle soundness has been derived rather than used as a premise.

Set
\[
 S_N(p,\gamma)=V_{0,N}(p)+V_{1,N}(p,\gamma),
 \qquad
 S(p,\gamma)=V_0(p)+V_\gamma(p).
\]
All four summands are nonnegative because, by their definitions, they are stationary Poisson energies.  The uniform energy convergence in Theorem \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\), whose compact domain is supplied by the rate-membership and staffing-window assumptions, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 r_N
 &:=\sup_{p\in\mathcal P,\,|\gamma|\leq G}
       |S_N(p,\gamma)-S(p,\gamma)|\\
 &\leq
 \sup_{p\in\mathcal P}|V_{0,N}(p)-V_0(p)|
 +\sup_{p\in\mathcal P,\,|\gamma|\leq G}
       |V_{1,N}(p,\gamma)-V_\gamma(p)|
 \longrightarrow0 .                                           \tag{1}
\end{aligned}
\]
For all \(x,y\geq0\),
\[
 |\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}|^2
 =\frac{|x-y|^2}{(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})^2}
 \leq |x-y|,                                                   \tag{2}
\]
where the case \(x=y=0\) follows directly.  By the definitions of \(J_N\) and the capacity--precision objective \(J\), their staffing terms \(c_M\gamma\) cancel.  Consequently, (1)--(2) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Delta_N
 &:=\sup_{p\in\mathcal P,\,|\gamma|\leq G}
       |J_N(p,\gamma)-J(p,\gamma)|\\
 &\leq c_I z_\alpha\sqrt{r_N}
 \longrightarrow0 .                                           \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
The multiplier in (3) is finite and positive: \(c_I>0\) by the information-cost assumption, while \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) implies \(1-\alpha/2\in(1/2,1)\), so \(z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)\in(0,\infty)\).  Thus (3) is uniform over the entire rate and staffing domain.

Fix \(p\in\mathcal P\) and write
\[
 \mu(p)=\inf_{|\gamma|\leq G}J(p,\gamma).
\]
Under the supplied input name, sound interval oracle, and returned certificate appearing in the theorem's conditional premise, Theorem \(\mathrm{oracle\mbox{-}conditional\mbox{-}capacity\mbox{-}certificate}\) applies to the definitions of the interval oracle, certificate algorithm, and capacity certificate.  It yields
\[
 L_\epsilon\leq\mu(p)
 \leq J(p,\gamma_\epsilon)
 \leq U_\epsilon,
 \qquad
 U_\epsilon-L_\epsilon\leq\epsilon .                          \tag{4}
\]
In particular,
\[
 J(p,\gamma_\epsilon)-\mu(p)
 \leq U_\epsilon-L_\epsilon
 \leq\epsilon .                                                \tag{5}
\]
The uniform comparison (3) also gives
\[
 \inf_{|\gamma|\leq G}J_N(p,\gamma)
 \geq \inf_{|\gamma|\leq G}\{J(p,\gamma)-\Delta_N\}
 =\mu(p)-\Delta_N,                                             \tag{6}
\]
and, because the certificate guarantees \(\gamma_\epsilon\in[-G,G]\),
\[
 J_N(p,\gamma_\epsilon)
 \leq J(p,\gamma_\epsilon)+\Delta_N.                           \tag{7}
\]
Subtracting (6) from (7) and applying (5) proves
\[
\begin{aligned}
 J_N(p,\gamma_\epsilon)
 -\inf_{|\gamma|\leq G}J_N(p,\gamma)
 &\leq J(p,\gamma_\epsilon)-\mu(p)+2\Delta_N\\
 &\leq\epsilon+2\Delta_N.                                    \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
The number \(\Delta_N\) does not depend on the selected \(p\), and (3) gives \(2\Delta_N=o(1)\).  Taking the supremum over \(p\in\mathcal P\) in (8) therefore proves the claimed uniform \(\epsilon+o(1)\) finite-system regret bound.  Every use of \(\gamma_\epsilon\) remains conditional on the supplied sound oracle and its certificate; hence the argument makes no unconditional model-specific oracle or staffing claim.

Fix \(\lambda,\tau>0\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), and regard \(\nu\geq0\) as the parameter of the continuous extension.  Write
\[
 d=\lambda+\tau,\qquad D_\nu=d+\nu,
 \qquad q_\nu=\frac{\lambda(\tau+\nu)}{d+\nu}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Then \(D_\nu\to d\) and \(q_\nu\to q_0=\lambda\tau/d\).  The treatment drift and generator are
\[
 b_{\nu,\gamma}(x)=-dx-\nu\min\{x,\gamma\},
 \qquad
 (\mathcal L_{\nu,\gamma}g)(x)
 =b_{\nu,\gamma}(x)g'(x)+q_\nu g''(x).
 \tag{2}
\]
Consequently \(b_{\nu,\gamma}\to-dx\) uniformly on compact subsets of \(\mathbb R\), and at \(\nu=0\) equation (2) is exactly the control generator \(\mathcal L_0\).

We also verify convergence of the stationary objects rather than inferring it solely from the generator.  Let \(r_{\nu,\gamma}\) denote the unnormalized density appearing in the definition of \(\pi_\gamma\), with \(D\) and \(q\) replaced by \(D_\nu\) and \(q_\nu\).  Pointwise in \(x\),
\[
 r_{\nu,\gamma}(x)\longrightarrow
 r_0(x):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{d x^2}{2q_0}\right).
 \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, on \(x\leq\gamma\) this follows from the first quadratic piece, while on \(x>\gamma\) both terms involving \(\nu\gamma\) vanish.  Choose any fixed \(\bar\nu>0\).  Continuity and positivity of \(q_\nu\) on \([0,\bar\nu]\) give constants \(0<q_-\leq q_\nu\leq q_+<\infty\).  On the left piece,
\[
 r_{\nu,\gamma}(x)
 \leq \exp\!\left(-\frac{d x^2}{2q_+}\right),
 \tag{4}
\]
whereas on the right piece Young's inequality gives a constant \(C_\gamma<\infty\), independent of \(\nu\in[0,\bar\nu]\), such that
\[
 -\frac{d x^2}{2q_\nu}-\frac{\nu\gamma x}{q_\nu}
 +\frac{\nu\gamma^2}{2q_\nu}
 \leq -\frac{d x^2}{4q_+}+C_\gamma.
 \tag{5}
\]
Thus \((1+|x|^2)r_{\nu,\gamma}(x)\) has a common integrable Gaussian envelope.  Dominated convergence applied first to the normalizing constants and then to the first two moments proves
\[
 \pi_{\nu,\gamma}\longrightarrow\pi_0
 \quad\hbox{in weighted \(L^1(1+|x|^2)\)},
 \qquad
 m_{\nu,\gamma}:=\int x\pi_{\nu,\gamma}(x)\,dx\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{6}
\]
Here the normalized version of \(r_0\) is \(\mathcal N(0,q_0/d)=\pi_0\).  Equations (2), (3), and (6) give the asserted reduction of the stationary treatment diffusion to the stationary control Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion.

It remains to pass the Poisson energy to the limit.  If \(y>x\), monotonicity and the one-Lipschitz property of \(z\mapsto\min\{z,\gamma\}\) imply
\[
 -(d+\nu)(y-x)
 \leq b_{\nu,\gamma}(y)-b_{\nu,\gamma}(x)
 \leq-d(y-x).
 \tag{7}
\]
Couple two solutions of the diffusion in (2), started at \(y\) and \(x\), with the same Brownian motion.  Their difference has no martingale part, so (7) and integration of the resulting scalar differential inequalities yield
\[
 e^{-(d+\nu)t}(y-x)
 \leq X_t^y-X_t^x
 \leq e^{-dt}(y-x).
 \tag{8}
\]
The centered resolvent
\[
 \bar h_{\nu,\gamma}(x)
 =\int_0^\infty
 \{\mathbb E_xX_t-m_{\nu,\gamma}\}\,dt
 \tag{9}
\]
is finite by (8).  Integrating the difference quotients in (8), and then letting \(y\downarrow x\), gives
\[
 \frac1{d+\nu}\leq \bar h_{\nu,\gamma}'(x)\leq\frac1d.
 \tag{10}
\]
The semigroup identity applied to (9) gives
\(-\mathcal L_{\nu,\gamma}\bar h_{\nu,\gamma}=x-m_{\nu,\gamma}\).  After subtraction of its stationary mean, uniqueness of the centered Poisson solution in Theorem \(\mathrm{diffusion\mbox{-}poisson}\) identifies \(\bar h_{\nu,\gamma}\) with the flux construction \(h_\gamma\).  In particular,
\[
 \sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\left|h_\gamma'(x)-\frac1d\right|
 \leq \frac1d-\frac1{d+\nu}
 =\frac{\nu}{d(d+\nu)}.
 \tag{11}
\]
Because \(\pi_{\nu,\gamma}\) is a probability density, (11) implies
\[
 \int\{h_\gamma'(x)\}^2\pi_{\nu,\gamma}(x)\,dx
 \longrightarrow\frac1{d^2}.
 \tag{12}
\]
Combining (1) and (12) proves
\[
 V_\gamma
 =2q_\nu\int\{h_\gamma'(x)\}^2\pi_{\nu,\gamma}(x)\,dx
 \longrightarrow \frac{2q_0}{d^2}
 =\frac{2\lambda\tau}{(\lambda+\tau)^3}.
 \tag{13}
\]

We next prove the fixed-system reduction.  Fix \(N\), an arm \(\ell\in\{0,1\}\), and an interior implemented capacity in the treatment arm.  By the two generator assumptions, every adjacent birth and death rate needed for irreducibility is positive.  Hence the finite birth--death chain is irreducible and has the stationary law \(\rho_{\ell,N}\).  On the scaled lattice define
\[
 f_{\ell,N}(x)=x-\mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}X_{\ell,N},
 \qquad
 -G_{\ell,N}u_{\ell,N}=f_{\ell,N},
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}u_{\ell,N}=0.
 \tag{14}
\]
Existence and uniqueness in (14) follow because the null space of the irreducible finite-state generator consists of the constants and \(f_{\ell,N}\) has stationary mean zero.  This is the exact prelimit Poisson solution used in Lemma \(\mathrm{finite\mbox{-}chain\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}controls}\).

Let \(r_N(x,y)\) be the transition rate from \(x\) to \(y\) for the scaled chain and put
\[
 c_{\ell,N}(x)
 =\sum_{y\ne x}r_N(x,y)
 \{u_{\ell,N}(y)-u_{\ell,N}(x)\}^2.
 \tag{15}
\]
Dynkin's identity and (14) give the square-integrable jump martingale
\[
 M_T=u_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(T))-u_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(0))
      +\int_0^T f_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(t))\,dt,
 \qquad
 \langle M\rangle_T=\int_0^T c_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(t))\,dt.
 \tag{16}
\]
Stationarity and the generator product identity
\[
 G_{\ell,N}(u^2)-2uG_{\ell,N}u
 =\sum_{y\ne x}r_N(x,y)\{u(y)-u(x)\}^2
 \tag{17}
\]
show that the exact stationary Poisson energy is
\[
 V_{\ell,N}
 :=\mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}c_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N})
 =-2\mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}
   \{u_{\ell,N}G_{\ell,N}u_{\ell,N}\}
 =2\mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}
   \{u_{\ell,N}f_{\ell,N}\}.
 \tag{18}
\]
The birth--death chain is reversible by detailed balance.  Lemma \(\mathrm{finite\mbox{-}chain\mbox{-}poisson\mbox{-}controls}\) bounds its spectral gap below by \(d>0\).  Applying its finite spectral expansion to the bounded function \(c_{\ell,N}\) therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\!\left{
 \frac1T\int_0^T c_{\ell,N}(X_{\ell,N}(t))\,dt
 \right}
 \leq
 \frac{2\operatorname{Var}_{\rho_{\ell,N}}(c_{\ell,N})}{dT}.
 \tag{19}
\]
Thus
\[
 T^{-1}\langle M\rangle_T\longrightarrow V_{\ell,N}
 \quad\hbox{in probability as \(T\to\infty\)}.
 \tag{20}
\]

For clarity, we derive the martingale limit from (20).  For fixed \(\xi\in\mathbb R\), set
\[
 \Psi_T(\xi)=\int_0^T\sum_{y\ne X_{t-}}r_N(X_{t-},y)
 \left[
 e^{i\xi\{u_{\ell,N}(y)-u_{\ell,N}(X_{t-})\}/\sqrt T}
 -1-\frac{i\xi\{u_{\ell,N}(y)-u_{\ell,N}(X_{t-})\}}{\sqrt T}
 \right]dt.
 \tag{21}
\]
The state space, all rates, and \(u_{\ell,N}\) are bounded because \(N\) is fixed.  Taylor's formula, (16), and (20) consequently imply
\[
 \Psi_T(\xi)
 =-\frac{\xi^2}{2T}\langle M\rangle_T+O(T^{-1/2})
 \longrightarrow-\frac{\xi^2V_{\ell,N}}2
 \quad\hbox{in probability}.
 \tag{22}
\]
A direct jump-product calculation shows that
\[
 Z_T(\xi)=\exp\{i\xi M_T/\sqrt T-\Psi_T(\xi)\}
 \tag{23}
\]
is a mean-one martingale: at a transition \(x\to y\) its multiplicative jump is the exponential in (21), and subtracting the corresponding transition-rate compensator makes its drift zero.  Moreover, \(1-\cos z\leq z^2/2\) and finiteness of the state space give \(\sup_T|Z_T(\xi)|<\infty\), while \(|e^{\Psi_T(\xi)}|\leq1\).  Hence (22), bounded convergence in probability, and \(\mathbb E Z_T(\xi)=1\) yield
\[
 \mathbb E\exp(i\xi M_T/\sqrt T)
 =\mathbb E\{Z_T(\xi)e^{\Psi_T(\xi)}\}
 \longrightarrow e^{-\xi^2V_{\ell,N}/2}.
 \tag{24}
\]
Thus \(M_T/\sqrt T\) converges in distribution to \(\mathcal N(0,V_{\ell,N})\).  Since \(u_{\ell,N}\) is bounded, the endpoint term in (16), divided by \(\sqrt T\), converges to zero.  We have therefore proved the explicit finite-state occupation limit
\[
 \frac1{\sqrt T}\int_0^T
 \{X_{\ell,N}(t)-\mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}X_{\ell,N}\}\,dt
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \mathcal N(0,V_{\ell,N}).
 \tag{25}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 \sqrt{NT}\left[
 \frac1T\int_0^T\frac{K_{\ell,N}(t)}N\,dt
 -\mathbb E_{\rho_{\ell,N}}\frac{K_{\ell,N}}N
 \right]
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \mathcal N(0,V_{\ell,N}).
 \tag{26}
\]
The energy is strictly positive: if (18) were zero, every edge difference of \(u_{\ell,N}\) would vanish; irreducibility would make \(u_{\ell,N}\) constant, contradicting (14) because the coordinate function is nonconstant.

As a smallest-instance check, take \(N=2\) and the interior treatment capacity \(M_N=1\).  The birth rates are \(2\lambda,\lambda,0\), and the death rates are \(0,\tau+\nu,2\tau+\nu\).  The unnormalized stationary weights are
\[
 1,qquad \frac{2\lambda}{\tau+\nu},qquad
 \frac{2\lambda^2}{(\tau+\nu)(2\tau+\nu)},
 \tag{27}
\]
all strictly positive.  If \(A_k=\sum_{j=0}^k\rho_{1,2}(j)f_{1,2}(j)\), then exact flux summation of (14) gives
\[
 u_{1,2}(x_{k+1})-u_{1,2}(x_k)
 =-\frac{A_k}{\rho_{1,2}(k)B_k},
 \qquad
 V_{1,2}=2\sum_{k=0}^1\frac{A_k^2}{\rho_{1,2}(k)B_k}>0.
 \tag{28}
\]
Indeed, \(A_0<0\), and centering gives \(A_1=-\rho_{1,2}(2)f_{1,2}(2)<0\).  Thus the smallest interior chain exhibits neither degeneracy nor a boundary exception to (25).

Equations (25)--(26) use the common fixed arm size and the stationary homogeneous generators imposed here.  Lemma \(\mathrm{boutilier\mbox{-}anchor\mbox{-}scope}\) records that the cited model permits distinct fixed arm populations and a separately specified capacity and presents its fixed-system occupation and many-system fluid limits separately.  The calculation above is therefore an internal reduction for the present equal-arm subclass; compatibility supplies no logical transfer of this positive result to that broader class.
